catalyst.event: The P&C catastrophe cycle: a heavy loss year is what produces the rate filings that drive the following two years of underwriting margin. Allstate disclosed $1.43bn pre-tax / $1.13bn after-tax of July-August 2026 cat losses and the shares have fallen 17.2% from their 277.22 high.
catalyst.action: wait for 217.00, then accumulate in thirds; expect more monthly cat disclosures before the Atlantic season ends 2026-11-30 and treat each one as a chance to buy a lower tranche, not as news

thesis: Allstate has repriced by roughly eleven times the loss it actually took. The 2026-09-17 press release discloses $748m pre-tax / $591m after-tax of August catastrophe losses across 21 events, half of them from a single wind-and-hail storm, and $1.43bn pre-tax / $1.13bn after-tax for July and August together. Against 257.42m shares that after-tax loss is **$4.39 per share**. The stock has fallen from 277.22 to 229.50, **$47.72 per share** — 10.9x the realised loss, or about $13.3bn of market value against $1.13bn of actual damage. The excess is a forward judgement that the elevated-cat regime is permanent. That judgement may be right, which is why it is priced into the bear case below rather than argued away; but a personal-lines carrier with 216 million policies in force is the entity that *raises rates* in response to a bad cat year, and the P&C cycle has always turned that into the next two years of margin.
key_risk: The invalidation is regulatory, not a price move: if the states that matter most for cat exposure refuse or materially delay Allstate's rate filings for two consecutive renewal cycles, the loss cost is permanent rather than recoverable and the thesis is wrong regardless of where the shares trade. Watch the approved-rate disclosures in the quarterly supplements. Second risk, and the reason for waiting: the Atlantic season runs to 2026-11-30 and Allstate discloses catastrophe losses **monthly**, so there are at least two more of these releases before the season is over.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is that this is not a one-off at all — that cat severity has structurally reset, every year now carries a billion dollars of losses above plan, and the de-rating is the market correctly capitalising a permanent earnings reduction. Take it at face value: $1.1bn a year of permanent after-tax impairment at a 12x multiple is about $13.2bn, or $51 per share off the 277.22 high — which lands at roughly 226. In other words **the 229.50 price already is the full structural-impairment case**, and there is no margin of safety in buying it here. That is precisely why the entry is 217.00 and not the market, and why the bear case is set lower still at 195.00 to allow for reserve strengthening beyond one year's worth. Positioning also argues against: insiders sold roughly $87.6m over the past twelve months with no open-market buying.
